phase1.intro:
Everything up to now has been static once it's drawn. Animation is the storefront's moving window display.

Where should we start?

topics.buttonText: How do the Transition classes work?
dialogue: JavaFX's transition classes each animate one property over time: [[term:TranslateTransition]] moves a node, FadeTransition changes opacity, RotateTransition spins, ScaleTransition resizes. All share the same recipe: construct with a Duration and target node, set the end state, then call play() — [[key:nothing animates until play() is called]].

stickyNote.flavor: ▶️ nothing moves until play() is called
stickyNote.definition: TranslateTransition, FadeTransition, RotateTransition, ScaleTransition each animate one property. All need play() called to actually run.

topics.buttonText: When do I need Timeline instead of a Transition?
dialogue: For anything more custom, [[term:Timeline]] is the general-purpose tool: a sequence of KeyFrame objects, each a point in time paired with what should be true at that instant (`new KeyFrame(Duration.seconds(2), new KeyValue(node.xProperty(), 300))`). A Timeline can hold many KeyFrames and interpolate smoothly between them.

stickyNote.flavor: 🎞️ multiple points in time, smoothly interpolated
stickyNote.definition: Timeline holds a sequence of KeyFrames (a time + a target value), interpolating smoothly between them for animations more complex than a single Transition.

topics.buttonText: What's actually driving the animation timing?
dialogue: [[fun:None of this runs on a thread you manage]] — JavaFX drives every animation off its own internal render pulse, roughly 60 times a second, updating the property a tiny bit each pulse. You never write a loop or a Thread.sleep() for this.

stickyNote.flavor: 🕐 ~60 times a second, no manual loop needed
stickyNote.definition: JavaFX animations run off an internal render pulse (~60fps), updating properties incrementally — no manual loop or Thread.sleep() required.

phase1.output: (Window with animating shapes — rectangles moving, circles fading, squares rotating, etc.)
phase1.openingDialogue: Animation classes animate one property at a time with play(), or use Timeline for multiple KeyFrames — all driven by JavaFX's own render pulse. ▶️

phase2.errorMessage: (Rectangle appears but doesn't animate — no movement!)
phase2.explanation:
[[warn:the rectangle sits there, fully visible, completely motionless]] — no error, because nothing about the code is actually wrong except one missing call.

A TranslateTransition was built and fully configured — duration set, target node set, destination coordinates set — [[key:but play() was never called]]. Every transition class in JavaFX follows the same build-then-trigger pattern you've now seen twice already this unit (Alert, Stage): configuring an object completely doesn't make anything happen on its own. Something always has to explicitly say "go."

phase3.openingDialogue: Animation — bring your UI to life! 🎬

mcq.question:
You need a circle to move right, then immediately turn red, then fade out — three distinct stages in sequence. Which tool fits best?

A) A single TranslateTransition, since all animation classes handle multiple properties automatically
B) Three separate transitions running simultaneously with no coordination
C) A Timeline with multiple KeyFrames marking each stage's timing and target state
D) A for-loop that manually updates the circle's position, color, and opacity

phase4.selfChallenge:
Write a JavaFX program with:
1. A Circle (radius 30) that moves horizontally across the screen
2. A Button "Start Animation" that starts the movement
3. A Button "Stop Animation" that stops and resets

Use TranslateTransition with duration 2 seconds, from X=0 to X=300.
The animation should auto-reverse and loop indefinitely.

phase5.trivia: [[fun:JavaFX animations are driven by the same internal render pulse the rest of the scene graph uses to redraw]], firing roughly 60 times a second — there's no separate animation clock running on its own schedule. That's also why heavy computation on the JavaFX thread can visibly stutter an animation: they're both competing for the same pulse.
